rv.q: “You’re In the Band,” the best number in the show, is a spirited audition piece that allows Dewey (and a delighted audience) to discover the amazing depth of talent in his classroom.
It worked for the movie, and wow, does it work on Broadway, a double jolt of adrenaline and sugar to inspire the most helicoptered of tots to play hooky and go shred an ax.
You keep waiting for a really great rock number that never quite arrives, a sticky but repetitive ditty called "Stick it to the Man" notwithstanding.
They supply a joyous blast of defiant analog vitality in a manufactured digital world.
The kids are definitely all right in Andrew Lloyd Webber’s enjoyable show.
In the meantime, family audiences should be grateful for a Lloyd Webber show that only wants to have fun and hopes that you do, too.
The show works because it doesn't condescend to children or pander to parents.
Webber blasted the theatrical doors down to let rock in with such shows as 'Jesus Christ Superstar' and 'Cats' but how could he handle this assignment? Not too badly, it turns out.
Like the victims of those enslaved warriors, I felt pummelled by the experience.

Nonetheless, were it not for Russo, MacKenzie, Niederauer, Dolan, Parker, Melucci and their knee-high-to-grasshopper compatriots, musical lovers wanting to watch Broadway school teachers interact with pupils might be better off right now at either Matilda or The King and I.

And that means that despite the contributions of its famous composer, Andrew Lloyd Webber, “School of Rock” has to settle for reduced status as another formulaic attempt by Broadway to capitalize on a popular movie of fairly recent vintage.
School of Rock lacks for some of the mayhem of Matilda, the dash of Spring Awakening, the pathos of Billy Elliot.
School of Rock is a big, beautiful blast of musical comedy from start to finish.
Broadway musicals can still surprise, delight, and rock out with the best of them
School of Rock – The Musical is full of both hard-charging rock n roll and supremely catchy melodies.

Essentially a modern version of 'The Music Man,' it charts how out-of-work musician Dewey Finn (Alex Brightman) lands a gig as a substitute teacher at a snobby prep school and turns his class into a garage band, giving the children self-confidence in the process...The dozen or so children are wildly talented and absolutely adorable.
If the children are in fact our future, School of Rock suggests we’re in pretty good hands.
Andrew Lloyd Webber's first new work for Broadway in a decade is an otherwise workaday screen-to-stage adaptation, with a generous lead actor and faithful, if prosaic book.
Missing completely is that anarchic edge of comedy.

cn.t: Critics find this energetic adaptation enjoyable if workmanlike, with Lloyd Webber's solid rock score and especially the talented young musicians earning praise, though some feel the material plays it safe.

vs.sum: The Winter Garden Theatre offers excellent legroom and spacious seating, making it one of the most comfortable venues on Broadway. Sightlines are generally good, though some side seats may have partial obstructions. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historical charm and garden-themed decor, while facilities are average with some potential for lines at restrooms.

acc.note: 20 wheelchair spaces (largest of Shubert theaters). 16 aisle transfer seats. Infrared devices available.
